The wisest man in Athens built his entire philosophy on admitting he knew nothing. Artificial intelligence was built to never admit that.

Hi, this is Markus and I will explain this meme to you.

The Oracle at Delphi once declared that no one in Athens was wiser than Socrates. Socrates did not believe it. He walked through the city interviewing politicians, poets, and craftsmen, certain one would prove the Oracle wrong. Every one was confident about justice, beauty, courage, the good life. Every one, pressed with a few simple questions, collapsed into contradiction. They did not know that they knew nothing.

Socrates concluded his wisdom was not knowledge. It was the absence of false confidence. He called it aporia, a state of puzzlement that keeps inquiry alive. Not knowing was the precondition for thinking.

Now put a chatbot in that room. Ask it about justice, beauty, the good life. It answers immediately, fluently, with total authority, whether or not a word is true. This is not lying. Lying requires knowing the truth and choosing to say something else. The philosopher Harry Frankfurt had a better word for it: bullshit. Bullshit is speech produced with total indifference to truth. The bullshitter is not thinking about the facts. He is thinking about how convincing he sounds.

Large language models are bullshit generators in the literal sense Frankfurt intended. They are built to predict the next plausible word, not to track truth. Confidence is not a byproduct of their design, it is the product. A model that said "I am not sure" whenever unsure would feel broken to most users, so that habit gets trained out. The result industrializes the posture Socrates dismantled: certainty without justification, at scale, all day, every day.

Socrates treated not knowing as an opening, the start of a conversation that could go somewhere true. The chatbot treats not knowing as a gap to smooth over with the most statistically likely sentence. One produces wisdom through confessing ignorance. The other produces authority by concealing it.

Developmental psychologists call this the continuity of self-concept problem, the question of how a person at age eight and that same person at thirty count as one identity at all. Derek Parfit's work on personal identity argued that psychological connectedness, overlapping chains of memory, belief and desire, matters more than any fixed essence, so a kid drawn to bright, chaotic imagery and an adult who inks that same imagery onto skin are linked by continuous strands of preference rather than sameness of substance.

The tattoo research itself points somewhere concrete. Studies on body art motivation, including work published in the journal Body Image, consistently find self-expression and identity narrative as the top reported reasons people get tattooed, ahead of group affiliation or spontaneity. The skin becomes an externalized autobiography, a durable record of taste and memory that most other markers of self don't allow.

There's also a nostalgia mechanism worth naming. Nostalgic recall, studied extensively by Constantine Sedikides and colleagues, reliably boosts perceived meaning in life and social connectedness by reactivating positive affect tied to earlier developmental periods. Choosing childhood-coded imagery as permanent adult art is a documented way people anchor identity continuity against the disorientation of aging and change.

What's the earliest thing you loved that still shows up in who you are now?

In 2024, an unsuspecting reality television contestant completely shattered the traditional American Idol mold by screaming their way through Drowning Pool's defining 2001 nu-metal anthem 'Bodies'. The mainstream reality singing landscape, dominated by polished pop vocals and acoustic country ballads, was genuinely unprepared for a blistering dose of heavy music on a network stage. Originally released on Drowning Pool's debut album Sinner via Wind-up Records, the song is a foundational pillar of the aggressive, early-2000s rock movement. Bringing this specific track to a judging panel consisting of Luke Bryan, Katy Perry, and Lionel Richie created a brilliant, jarring clash of musical cultures that immediately went viral.

The mechanics behind performing such an aggressive track in a sterile television environment require an entirely different type of vocal conditioning than a standard pop ballad. Nu-metal screaming relies on intense diaphragm control and false-chord vocal techniques to produce the gritty, distorted sound without causing permanent damage to the vocal folds. The contestant had to perfectly execute the song's legendary, tension-building introâmoving from a menacing, repetitive whisper into an explosive, guttural roar as the chorus drops.

While Drowning Pool's original version peaked at #6 on the Billboard Mainstream Rock chart and went multi-platinum, this surreal performance brought the track to an entirely new demographic. The viral clip generated millions of views across social media, proving that the visceral, aggressive energy of nu-metal still commands intense attention. It stands as a hilarious and triumphant moment in modern television, showing that alternative heavy music can still crash the mainstream party when least expected.

I've been a graphic designer for 25 years. Sometimes professionally. Mostly unprofessionally because I'm bad at being employed. I gave up my Adobe subscription last year because they veered headfirst into generative AI tools, and I was fed up with the predatory pricing structure that pioneered the techno feudalism movement. We will own nothing and we will be happy. 

I dumped Microsoft and installed Linux so I had to change the graphics programs like Affinity that I'd already switched to. I know there's a workaround to run it on Linux but I am not really in any headspace for figuring that stuff out. In fact, I am struggling with Gimp but fortunately I'm more of a bezier broad. Inkspace is ok but has its pitfalls. Nothing is easy when it comes to computer aided design for me these days.

So I stitch. Generative AI can't compete with me when I make pictures with my hands, thread and cloth. 

You can make pictures with generative AI but they will never be effective communication. You can replace graphic designers, illustrators and visual artists with generative AI but your pictures will not have context or the active interchange of hundreds of thousands of years of human thought and meaning. If I had to start all over again from 0 followers today, these are the things I'd focus on.

ð Stop waiting for the perfect setup

I started my Bookstagram with no setup at all.

No fancy bookshelf.
No aesthetic reading nook.
No expensive camera.

Most of my early videos were filmed with stacks of books behind me as the background.

I didn't wait until things looked perfect. I started with what I had and improved as I went.

If you're waiting for the perfect setup, this is your sign to start anyway.

ð Pick 2â3 content pillars

Don't try to create every type of book content.
Choose a few topics you genuinely enjoy and can consistently talk about.

For me, content became much easier when I stopped trying to do everything and focused on a few formats that felt natural.

ð Post reels from Day 1. If you can post trial reels as well.

Your first reel won't be great.

Neither will your tenth.

But every reel teaches you something about hooks, editing, storytelling, and what your audience enjoys.
The fastest way to improve is to start.

ð Join reading challenges

This helped me more than any growth tip.

When you start a new page, you're excited. But after a few weeks, when the views are low, motivation starts to disappear.

Reading challenges gave me a reason to keep showing up even when the numbers didn't.

ð Build relationships

Bookstagram is a community.

Some of my favorite opportunities, recommendations, and friendships came from genuinely connecting with other readers.

Support others, leave meaningful comments, and be part of the conversation.

Most creators don't quit because they aren't capable.
